ER and EER Modelling

Chapters 3 & 4 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 3.3–3.13, 3.16, 3.17, 3.22, 3.26, 4.2, 4.6, 4.7, 4.16–4.20. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

Conceptual design turns a page of requirements into a diagram that a non-programmer can check and a designer can map to tables. The ER model has entities, attributes and relationships; the EER model adds subclasses, specialization and categories. Most marks in this topic are lost on constraints, not shapes: which side each (min,max) goes on, total participation for weak entities, and disjointness and completeness on every specialization.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  Where ER modelling sits in database design

    Theory recap
    The four phases (Fig. 3.1)

    Requirements collection and analysis (data + functional requirements) →\rightarrow→ conceptual design (a high-level, DBMS-independent schema: the ER/EER diagram) →\rightarrow→ logical design / data-model mapping (ER →\rightarrow→ relations, Ch. 9) →\rightarrow→ physical design (indexes, storage). Users and designers can both read the conceptual schema, so it is where you check that every requirement is captured and nothing conflicts, before any table is created.

    The ER model describes the miniworld with three ideas: entities (things), attributes (their properties) and relationships (associations among things), plus structural constraints on the relationships. The EER (enhanced ER) model adds subclasses/superclasses, specialization/generalization and categories (union types).

    2  Entities, attributes, keys and value sets

    Theory recap

    Entities and attributes

    Definition: Entity, attribute, attribute value

    An entity is a thing or object in the miniworld with an independent existence: physical (a person, a car) or conceptual (a company, a job, a university course). Each entity is described by attributes, its properties (Name, Age, Salary). Each entity has a value for each of its attributes, e.g. the employee John Smith has Salary =30000=30000=30000.

    KindMeaningExample / ER symbol
    Simple (atomic)not divisible into meaningful partsSsn, Salary: plain oval
    Compositemade of component attributes, which may themselves be composite (a hierarchy)Name(Fname, Minit, Lname), Address(Street_address( Number, Street, Apt_no), City, State, Zip): oval with child ovals
    Single-valuedone value per entityAge of a person
    Multivalueda set of values per entity, possibly with lower/upper boundsLocations of a DEPARTMENT, College_degrees of a person: double oval
    Stored vs. derivedderived value is computable from other stored dataAge from Birth_date; Number_of_employees by counting: dashed oval
    Complexcomposite and multivalued nested arbitrarily; written with ( ) for composite and { } for multivalued{Address_phone( {Phone( Area_code, Phone_number)}, Address(…))} (Fig. 3.5)

    NULL values are used when (i) the attribute is not applicable to this entity (Apartment_number of a single-family house, College_degrees of a person with none), or (ii) the value is unknown: either it exists but is missing (a person’s Height not recorded) or it is not known whether it exists (Home_phone).

    Entity types, entity sets, keys and value sets

    Definition: Entity type and entity set

    An entity type is the schema (intension) for a collection of entities that share the same attributes: a name plus a list of attributes, e.g. EMPLOYEE(Name, Age, Salary). The entity set (extension) is the collection of all entities of that type in the database at a particular moment. An entity is one member of that set. The entity set is usually referred to by the same name as the type.

    Definition: Key attribute (uniqueness constraint)

    A key attribute of an entity type is an attribute (possibly composite) whose values are distinct for every entity in the entity set at every point in time. It is a property of the type (it must hold for every possible extension), not of today’s data. Drawn with its name underlined. An entity type may have several keys (CAR has Registration and Vehicle_id); a composite key must be minimal. An entity type with no key is a weak entity type.

    Superkey vs. candidate key vs. primary key

    TermDefinition
    SuperkeyAny set of attributes SSS such that no two entities (tuples) can ever agree on all of SSS. The set of all attributes is always a superkey. Adding attributes to a superkey gives a superkey.
    Candidate key (key)A minimal superkey: removing any attribute makes it stop being a superkey. There can be several.
    Primary keyThe one candidate key the designer chooses to identify entities/tuples (underlined; used by foreign keys). The others are alternate (unique) keys. Must not be NULL.

    Every candidate key is a superkey; not every superkey is a candidate key ({\{{Ssn, Name}\}} is a superkey, not a key, because {\{{Ssn}\}} alone already works). Primary ⊆\subseteq⊆ candidate ⊆\subseteq⊆ super, as sets of attribute sets.

    Counting superkeys

    Let the entity type have nnn attributes. A set SSS is a superkey iff it contains at least one candidate key.

    • One key KKK with kkk attributes: the other n−kn-kn−k attributes are free (in or out), so #superkeys=2 n−k\#\text{superkeys} = 2^{\,n-k}#superkeys=2n−k.

    • Several keys K1,…,KmK_1,\dots,K_mK1​,…,Km​: inclusion–exclusion over “S⊇KiS\supseteq K_iS⊇Ki​”:

      #superkeys=∑i2 n−∣Ki∣−∑i<j2 n−∣Ki∪Kj∣+∑i<j<l2 n−∣Ki∪Kj∪Kl∣−⋯\#\text{superkeys}=\sum_i 2^{\,n-|K_i|}-\sum_{i<j}2^{\,n-|K_i\cup K_j|}+\sum_{i<j<l}2^{\,n-|K_i\cup K_j\cup K_l|}-\cdots#superkeys=i∑​2n−∣Ki​∣−i<j∑​2n−∣Ki​∪Kj​∣+i<j<l∑​2n−∣Ki​∪Kj​∪Kl​∣−⋯

    How superkey counts go wrong

    Forgetting that each superkey must contain a whole key (a composite key {A,B}\{A,B\}{A,B} contributes only sets containing both); double counting supersets of two keys; counting the empty set; listing superkeys that are not supersets of any key. Show the formula and the arithmetic: the 2024 rubric gave only 1 of 3 marks for the bare number.

    Definition: Value set (domain)

    Each simple attribute AAA of entity type EEE is associated with a value set VVV: the set of values that may be assigned to AAA for each entity (e.g. Age: integers 16–70; Name: strings of letters). Formally an attribute is a function A:E→P(V)A: E\rightarrow P(V)A:E→P(V) (P(V)P(V)P(V) = power set of VVV) mapping each entity to a set of values: a single-valued attribute gives singletons, a multivalued one gives any subset, NULL is the empty set. For a composite attribute the value set is the Cartesian product V=P(V1)×⋯×P(Vn)V = P(V_1)\times\cdots\times P(V_n)V=P(V1​)×⋯×P(Vn​) of the components’ value sets.

    Attribute vs. value set: the attribute is the property (a named function on entities); the value set is the set of allowed values it may take. Several attributes can share one value set (Salary and Bonus both from positive decimals), and the attribute adds the meaning.

    3  Relationship types and their constraints

    Theory recap

    Relationship type, set and instance; degree; roles

    Definition: Relationship type, relationship set, relationship instance

    A relationship type RRR among nnn entity types E1,…,EnE_1,\dots,E_nE1​,…,En​ defines a set of associations among their entities (schema level). The relationship set is the current set of relationship instances ri=(e1,…,en)r_i=(e_1,\dots,e_n)ri​=(e1​,…,en​) with ej∈Eje_j\in E_jej​∈Ej​; mathematically a subset of E1×⋯×EnE_1\times\cdots\times E_nE1​×⋯×En​. Each EjE_jEj​ participates in RRR. Example: WORKS_FOR between EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT; instance (Smith,Research)(\text{Smith},\text{Research})(Smith,Research).

    • Degree = number of participating entity types: binary (2), ternary (3), …. (Do not confuse with the number of attributes.)
    • Relationships as attributes. A binary relationship can be viewed as a pair of inverse reference attributes: EMPLOYEE.Department (value set = the DEPARTMENT entity set) and DEPARTMENT.Employees (multivalued; value set = the power set of the EMPLOYEE entity set). This view underlies the functional data models (and object databases’ reference attributes).
    • Role names name the part each participating entity plays (EMPLOYEE plays employee, DEPARTMENT plays department in WORKS_FOR). They are optional when the entity types are distinct, and necessary when the same entity type participates more than once.
    • A recursive (self-referencing) relationship is one where the same entity type participates in different roles: SUPERVISION(supervisor: EMPLOYEE, supervisee: EMPLOYEE). Others: MENTORS between researchers, PREREQUISITE between courses, MARRIED_TO between persons, PART_OF between parts (bill of materials).

    Structural constraints: cardinality ratio and participation

    Definition: Cardinality ratio (binary)

    The maximum number of relationship instances an entity can participate in: 1:1, 1:N, N:1, M:N. Written as 1/N/M beside the diamond on each edge. In WORKS_FOR, DEPARTMENT:EMPLOYEE is 1:N: a department has many employees, an employee works for one department. The “1” is written on the DEPARTMENT edge because each employee is related to at most one department.

    Definition: Participation constraint (existence dependency)

    Whether every entity must participate: total participation (every entity of the type is in at least one instance; drawn as a double line) or partial (some; single line). Every EMPLOYEE must work for a department (total); not every employee manages one (partial in MANAGES).

    Together, cardinality ratio + participation are the structural constraints of a relationship.

    The (min, max) notation, and how it relates to 1:N

    Definition: (min, max) on a participation

    For each participation of EEE in RRR, a pair (min⁡,max⁡)(\min,\max)(min,max) with 0≤min⁡≤max⁡0\le\min\le\max0≤min≤max, max⁡≥1\max\ge 1max≥1: each entity e∈Ee\in Ee∈E must participate in at least min⁡\minmin and at most max⁡\maxmax relationship instances of RRR at all times. It is written on the edge next to EEE (the entity it constrains). min⁡=0\min=0min=0 means partial participation, min⁡≥1\min\ge1min≥1 means total; max⁡\maxmax may be a number or N.

    Read the bottom row as: “each EMPLOYEE works for at least 1 and at most 1 department; each DEPARTMENT has at least 4 and at most N employees” (Fig. 3.15). The max that looks like the “1” of the ratio sits on the opposite side.

    Ratio E1:E2E_1:E_2E1​:E2​ on edges (E1E_1E1​—1, E2E_2E2​—N)(min,max) beside E1E_1E1​(min,max) beside E2E_2E2​
    1:1(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)
    1:N (each E2E_2E2​ has ≤1\le1≤1 E1E_1E1​)(⋅,N)(\cdot,\text{N})(⋅,N)(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)
    M:N(⋅,N)(\cdot,\text{N})(⋅,N)(⋅,N)(\cdot,\text{N})(⋅,N)
    partial / total participation of EEE(0,⋅)(0,\cdot)(0,⋅)(1,⋅)(1,\cdot)(1,⋅) or higher
    The single most common deduction: (min,max) on the wrong side

    In Chen ratio notation the “1” of 1:N goes next to the entity that appears once; in (min,max) the pair next to EEE describes EEE’s own participation. So WORKS_FOR is N:1 as EMPLOYEE N—1 DEPARTMENT, but EMPLOYEE (1,1)—(1,N) DEPARTMENT. Never write a bare “1:N”, “N” or “1” when the question asks for (min,max): the GA2 rubric treats a non-pair label as a major mistake (grade C). Pick one convention and use it on every relationship; state it in an assumption if in doubt.

    Two notations compared (Ex. 3.8). Ratio+participation is compact, the standard Chen notation, and tells you how to map (1:N →\rightarrow→ FK on the N side), but it only distinguishes 0/1 and 1/many. (min,max) is more precise (“at least 4”, “at most 3”) and applies uniformly to n-ary relationships, but is less familiar, easy to put on the wrong side, and for n>2n>2n>2 does not tell you the key of the relationship.

    Attributes of relationship types, and where they can migrate

    A relationship type can have attributes: Hours of WORKS_ON, Start_date of MANAGES.

    Migration rule
    • 1:1: the attribute can migrate to either participating entity type (each entity is in at most one instance, so the value is determined by either side). Start_date of MANAGES can go to DEPARTMENT or EMPLOYEE.
    • 1:N: it can migrate only to the N-side entity type (each N-side entity is in at most one instance). Start_date of WORKS_FOR can go to EMPLOYEE, not DEPARTMENT.
    • M:N: it cannot migrate: its value is determined by the combination of the entities (Hours depends on the (employee, project) pair).

    Even when migration is allowed it is a design choice; conceptually the attribute belongs to the relationship. If the side receiving it has partial participation, the migrated attribute will be NULL for non-participants.

    Weak entity types

    Definition: Weak entity, owner, identifying relationship, partial key

    A weak entity type has no key attribute of its own. Its entities are identified by being related to a specific entity of an owner (identifying, parent) entity type through the identifying relationship type, combined with the weak entity’s partial key (discriminator): the attribute(s) that distinguish weak entities belonging to the same owner. Notation: weak entity = double rectangle; identifying relationship = double diamond; partial key = dashed underline; weak side has total participation (double line), (1,1) in (min,max), and the identifying relationship is 1:N or 1:1 owner-to-weak. Example: DEPENDENT(Name, Sex, Birth_date, Relationship) owned by EMPLOYEE via DEPENDENTS_OF; full identifier = (owner’s Ssn, Dependent Name).

    • A weak entity always has total participation in its identifying relationship (existence dependency), but total participation does not make an entity weak: DRIVER_LICENSE cannot exist without a PERSON, yet it has its own key License_number, so it is strong.
    • Weak entities can be nested (an owner may itself be weak), and may have several owners with an identifying relationship of degree >2>2>2 (INTERVIEW owned by CANDIDATE and COMPANY, Fig. 3.19).
    • Alternative: a multivalued composite attribute (Dependents of EMPLOYEE). Prefer the weak entity if it participates independently in other relationships, or has many attributes.
    Weak-entity marks the rubrics take off

    Partial key underlined solid (minor); weak entity drawn as a single box / identifying relationship as a single diamond (minor); weak entity without an identifying relationship to an owner, or with min 0 on the weak side of it (major, logical flaw); weak entity with no partial key at all (major).

    4  ER diagram notation and the COMPANY schema

    Theory recap

    Full notation legend (Fig. 3.14)

    Naming conventions and diagram conventions (Ex. 3.14, 3.15)

    • Entity type names: singular nouns in UPPERCASE (EMPLOYEE, not EMPLOYEES): the name applies to each individual entity. Relationship type names: UPPERCASE verbs (WORKS_FOR). Attribute names: Initial capital (Birth_date). Role names: lowercase (supervisor).
    • From a requirements narrative: nouns →\rightarrow→ entity types, verbs →\rightarrow→ relationship types, nouns describing other nouns →\rightarrow→ attributes.
    • Choose relationship names so the diagram reads left-to-right / top-to-bottom (EMPLOYEE HAS_DEPENDENTS DEPENDENT reads top-down; DEPENDENTS_OF reads bottom-up).
    • Do not represent a relationship twice: once EMPLOYEE.Department is modelled as WORKS_FOR, remove the attribute (no foreign-key attributes in an ER diagram).

    Design choices: attribute, entity or relationship?

    • An attribute that is a reference to another entity type should become a relationship (Department of EMPLOYEE →\rightarrow→ WORKS_FOR); a pair of inverse attributes becomes one binary relationship.
    • An attribute that exists in several entity types, or has its own properties, can be promoted to an entity type (Department attribute of STUDENT, INSTRUCTOR, COURSE →\rightarrow→ entity DEPARTMENT with relationships).
    • Conversely, an entity type with a single attribute related to only one other entity type may be demoted to an attribute (DEPARTMENT with only Dname, related only to STUDENT).
    • Multivalued composite attribute vs. weak entity: weak entity if it takes part in other relationships.
    • Binary vs. ternary: see Section 5; do not split a ternary into binaries unless the semantics allow it.

    The COMPANY ER diagram (Fig. 3.2, constraints of Fig. 3.15)

    Requirements (Sec. 3.2): the company has DEPARTMENTs (unique Name and Number, several Locations, managed by one employee with a Start_date); a department CONTROLS PROJECTs (unique Name and Number, one Location); EMPLOYEEs (Ssn, Name, Address, Salary, Sex, Bdate) work for one department and work on several projects for some Hours each, and have a direct supervisor; DEPENDENTs (Name, Sex, Birth_date, Relationship) are kept for insurance.

    5  Relationships of degree higher than two

    Theory recap

    Ternary vs. three binaries

    SUPPLY(SUPPLIER, PART, PROJECT) holds (s,p,j)(s,p,j)(s,p,j) when supplier sss supplies part ppp to project jjj. Three binaries CAN_SUPPLY(s,p), USES(j,p), SUPPLIES(s,j) are not equivalent: from (s,p)(s,p)(s,p), (j,p)(j,p)(j,p), (s,j)(s,j)(s,j) you cannot conclude that sss supplies ppp to jjj (sss might supply ppp to another project and something else to jjj). The ternary records strictly more information.

    When can binaries replace a ternary?

    In general they cannot. The usual solution is to keep the ternary and any binary that has an independent meaning (CAN_SUPPLY: what a supplier is able to supply). Binaries that are mere projections of the ternary are redundant (TAUGHT_DURING, OFFERED_DURING in Fig. 3.18). Binaries can replace it only under extra constraints, e.g. if CAN_TEACH(instructor, course) is 1:1 then OFFERS(i, s, c) is derivable from the binaries. A ternary can also be modelled as a weak entity with no partial key and three identifying relationships (for binary-only tools), or as a strong entity with a surrogate key (Supply_id) and three N:1 relationships.

    Constraints on n-ary relationships

    • Ratio notation (1/M/N on each edge): a “1” on EiE_iEi​ means: for a fixed combination of the other entities, at most one EiE_iEi​ entity. With 1 on SUPPLIER and M, N on PROJECT, PART: each (project, part) pair has one supplier, so {j,p}\{j,p\}{j,p} is a key of the relationship set. Edges marked 1 are not needed in the key; if all are M/N the key is all three.
    • (min,max) notation: each entity takes part in at least min and at most max relationship instances (tuples). It constrains the counts but, for n>2n>2n>2, says nothing about the key. The two notations express different constraints; use both if both matter.
    Past paper (2023 End-Sem, Q7): exact (min,max) for ternary TEACHES(PROFESSOR, COURSE, STUDENT)

    Constraints: a course is taught by 1–2 professors and attended by 1–100 students; a professor teaches 0–3 courses; a student attends 0–6 courses. Give exact numbers, no N.

    Key reasoning

    An instance is a triple (p,c,s)(p,c,s)(p,c,s): “professor ppp teaches course ccc to student sss”. (min,max) of an entity counts the triples it appears in, not the courses.

    • COURSE (1,200)(1,200)(1,200). Min: at least 1 professor and 1 student, so at least 1 triple. Max: at most 2 professors ×\times× 100 students =200=200=200 triples (if each professor teaches every student).
    • PROFESSOR (0,300)(0,300)(0,300). Min 0 (may teach no course). Max: 3 courses, each with at most 100 students, 3×100=3003\times100=3003×100=300.
    • STUDENT (0,12)(0,12)(0,12). Min 0 (may attend no course). Max: 6 courses, each taught by at most 2 professors, 6×2=126\times2=126×2=12.

    Assumption to state: in a course with two professors a student may be taught by both (co-teaching). If instead each student in a course is taught by exactly one of its professors, COURSE becomes (1,100)(1,100)(1,100) and STUDENT (0,6)(0,6)(0,6), PROFESSOR stays (0,300)(0,300)(0,300). Writing (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) for PROFESSOR is the classic error: that counts courses, not relationship instances.

    6  Worked past-paper pattern: modifying an ER diagram · 2025 End-Sem, Q1

    Theory recap

    Given: RESEARCHER(ResearcherID, Name, Email, JoinDate) LEADS (1:N) PROJECT(ProjectID, Title, Domain); RESEARCHER DEVELOPS (M:N) ALGORITHM(AlgoName, Type); PROJECT USES (M:N) DATASET(DatasetID, Source, Size). Add: (a) mentorship: every junior researcher has exactly one mentor, who is also a researcher; a senior can supervise many juniors or none. (b) experimental logs: every instance where a researcher runs a specific algorithm on a specific dataset, with the resulting Accuracy_Score. (c) funding installments: an installment cannot exist without its project; identified by a Serial_No that repeats across projects, plus the Amount.

    Teal = additions. Notation kept as in the given diagram (1/M/N ratios, double line = total).

    Solution: Model answer

    (a) Recursive relationship MENTORS on RESEARCHER, roles mentor (1) and mentee (N). (min,max): mentor (0,N)(0,N)(0,N) (a senior supervises many or none), mentee (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Seniors have no mentor, so the mentee side is partial (min 0), not total. Why: only juniors must have one. If the question means every researcher is a junior or has a mentor, make it total (1,1)(1,1)(1,1).
    2. Alternative accepted design: specialize RESEARCHER into JUNIOR_RESEARCHER and SENIOR_RESEARCHER (disjoint, total) and put MENTORS between them with JUNIOR (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), SENIOR (0,N)(0,N)(0,N), which enforces “every junior has exactly one mentor” exactly.

    (b) Experimental runs. A plain ternary RUNS(RESEARCHER, ALGORITHM, DATASET) with attribute Accuracy_Score can hold only one instance per (researcher, algorithm, dataset) triple, because a relationship set is a set. “Log every instance” means repeated runs of the same triple, so model RUN as a weak entity with partial key Run_timestamp (or Run_no) and three identifying relationships (the book’s SUPPLY-as-weak-entity pattern, Fig. 3.17(c)); RUN has total participation (1,1) in each; owners (0,N)(0,N)(0,N).

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The same researcher may run the same algorithm on the same dataset more than once. Why: a log. If only the latest result is needed, the ternary relationship RUNS with Accuracy_Score suffices.

    (c) Installments. INSTALLMENT is a weak entity (double box), partial key Serial_No (dashed underline, repeats across projects), attribute Amount, identifying relationship HAS_INST (double diamond) with PROJECT 1 : N INSTALLMENT, INSTALLMENT total (1,1), PROJECT partial (0,N) (a new project may have received nothing yet). Full identifier: (ProjectID, Serial_No).

    7  EER: subclasses, superclasses and inheritance

    Theory recap
    Definition: Subclass, superclass, inheritance

    A subclass SSS of an entity type CCC (its superclass) is a subgrouping of CCC’s entities that needs separate representation: S⊆CS\subseteq CS⊆C at all times (the class/subclass or IS-A relationship: a SECRETARY IS-A EMPLOYEE). An entity in a subclass is the same real-world entity as in the superclass, in a specific role; it cannot exist only in the subclass. The subclass inherits all attributes and all relationships of the superclass (type inheritance) and may have its own specific (local) attributes and relationships.

    Two reasons to create a subclass: some attributes apply only to some entities (Typing_speed for SECRETARY); some relationships apply only to some entities (only SALARIED_EMPLOYEEs participate in BELONGS_TO a trade union).

    Specialization and generalization

    • Specialization (top-down): define a set of subclasses of an entity type on the basis of some distinguishing characteristic: {\{{SECRETARY, ENGINEER, TECHNICIAN}\}} of EMPLOYEE by job type; {\{{SALARIED_EMPLOYEE, HOURLY_EMPLOYEE}\}} by method of pay. An entity type can have several specializations.
    • Generalization (bottom-up): identify common features of several entity types and factor them into a superclass: CAR and TRUCK →\rightarrow→ VEHICLE (common Vehicle_id, Price, License_plate_no). Generalization is the inverse of specialization, and the book draws both the same way.

    Constraints on specialization/generalization

    ConstraintMeaning and notation
    Predicate-defined (condition-defined) subclassmembership decided by a condition on superclass attributes, written on the line: Job_type = ’Secretary’
    Attribute-defined specializationall subclasses defined by a condition on the same attribute (the defining attribute), written on the line from the superclass to the circle; disjoint if the attribute is single-valued
    User-definedno condition; the user places each entity in subclasses individually
    Disjointness: disjoint (d)an entity can be in at most one subclass
    Disjointness: overlapping (o)an entity may be in more than one subclass
    Completeness: totalevery superclass entity must be in some subclass: double line superclass–circle
    Completeness: partialan entity may belong to none of the subclasses: single line

    Disjointness and completeness are independent, giving four combinations: disjoint total, disjoint partial, overlapping total, overlapping partial. Generalized superclasses are usually total (the superclass was built from the subclasses).

    Insertion/deletion rules that follow

    Deleting an entity from a superclass deletes it from all its subclasses. Inserting into a superclass inserts it into every predicate-/attribute-defined subclass whose predicate it satisfies. Inserting into the superclass of a total specialization requires inserting it into at least one subclass.

    Attribute-defined, disjoint, partial: EMPLOYEE by Job_type (Fig. 4.4) and an overlapping total one

    Left: a secretary cannot also be an engineer (single-valued defining attribute), and an employee may have another job (partial). Right: a part can be both manufactured and purchased (o), and every part is one of them (total).

    Hierarchies, lattices, shared subclasses

    • Specialization hierarchy: every subclass has exactly one superclass (tree).
    • Specialization lattice: a subclass may be a subclass in more than one class/subclass relationship. Such a subclass is a shared subclass; e.g. ENGINEERING_MANAGER is a subclass of ENGINEER, MANAGER and SALARIED_EMPLOYEE.
    • Multiple inheritance: a shared subclass inherits from all its superclasses; an attribute inherited twice via different paths is included only once. Its entities are the intersection of the superclasses: an engineering manager must be an engineer and a manager and salaried.
    • A leaf node is a class with no subclasses. In a hierarchy or lattice an entity exists in the root and in some set of descendant (leaf or intermediate) classes.

    Union types (categories)

    Definition: Category (union type)

    A category is a subclass of the union of two or more superclasses that are different entity types: OWNER ⊆\subseteq⊆ PERSON ∪\cup∪ BANK ∪\cup∪ COMPANY. Drawn with a circle marked ∪\cup∪ joined to the superclasses and one subset-marked line to the category. A category entity inherits only the attributes of the one superclass it actually belongs to (selective inheritance). A category can be total (double line from circle to category: it holds the whole union) or partial (single line).

    Shared subclass (lattice)Category (union type)
    Membershipin all superclasses: intersectionin at least one superclass: union
    Inheritanceall attributes of all superclassesonly those of the superclass it belongs to
    Superclassesusually share a root, same keytypically different entity types, different keys
    Notationseveral subset-lines from the subclass to its superclasses / their circlesone circle with ∪\cup∪
    ExampleENGINEERING_MANAGEROWNER, REGISTERED_VEHICLE = CAR ∪\cup∪ TRUCK

    Category vs. generalization: generalizing CAR and TRUCK into VEHICLE means every car is a vehicle and the superclass holds the common key; a category REGISTERED_VEHICLE = CAR ∪\cup∪ TRUCK is right when the classes have different keys and only some (partial) or all (total) of them belong. A total category can often be redone as a generalization; prefer the category when the superclasses have different keys or are genuinely different things.

    EER notation legend and design choices

    Design choices (Sec. 4.5.2). Use a subclass only if it has specific attributes or specific relationships; otherwise a type attribute (Job_type) is enough and the subclasses can be dropped. Subclasses with few or no specific attributes can be merged into the superclass with a type attribute. Avoid union types unless needed. The d/o and total/partial choice must follow the miniworld and be stated as an assumption when the requirements are silent.

    What the IA2 / GA2 EER rubrics check

    Grade C (major mistake): a strong entity with no key, or a weak entity with no partial key; any relationship end with no label or with a non-pair label (“1:N”, “N”) when (min,max) is required; a min greater than its max; a weak entity with min 0 on the weak side of its identifying relationship, or with no identifying relationship; d where the diagram shows one entity in two subclasses (or o where it cannot); a subclass attached to anything other than its superclass; a dangling relationship line.
    Minor (3 or more drops to B): no multivalued and no composite attribute anywhere; wrong notation (weak entity not double box, identifying relationship not double diamond, partial key solid-underlined, no subset/triangle on the hierarchy, derived attribute not dashed); no written assumptions.
    Not penalised: names different from the key, layout, a consistent (min,max) convention on the opposite end, a defended d/o choice, up to two defensible min values.

    8  Chapter 3 exercises

    Textbook exercises

    3.3Define the basic ER termsE&N Ex. 3.3 · p. 96

    Define the following terms: entity, attribute, attribute value, relationship instance, composite attribute, multivalued attribute, derived attribute, complex attribute, key attribute, and value set (domain).

    Solution · written for this guide
    TermDefinitionCOMPANY example
    Entitya thing in the miniworld with an independent existence, physical or conceptualthe employee John Smith; the Research department
    Attributea particular property that describes an entity (or relationship)Name, Salary of EMPLOYEE
    Attribute valuethe value an attribute takes for one particular entitySalary of John Smith =30000=30000=30000
    Relationship instancean association (e1,…,en)(e_1,\dots,e_n)(e1​,…,en​) of one entity from each participating entity type(Smith, Research) in WORKS_FOR
    Composite attributean attribute divisible into smaller sub-parts (components) with independent meaning; components may themselves be compositeName(Fname, Minit, Lname)
    Multivalued attributean attribute that can hold a set of values for one entity (double oval)Locations of DEPARTMENT
    Derived attributean attribute whose value can be computed from other attributes or related entities (dashed oval)Number_of_employees of DEPARTMENT; Age from Bdate
    Complex attributecomposite and multivalued attributes nested to any depth; ( ) groups components, { } marks multivalued{Address_phone( {Phone( Area_code, Phone_number)}, Address(…))}
    Key attributean attribute (possibly composite) whose values are distinct for every entity of the entity set, in every state; underlinedSsn of EMPLOYEE; Number of DEPARTMENT
    Value set (domain)the set of values that may be assigned to an attribute for an entityAge: integers 16–70
    3.4Entity, entity type, entity setE&N Ex. 3.4 · p. 96

    What is an entity type? What is an entity set? Explain the differences among an entity, an entity type, and an entity set.

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Entity type: the schema (intension) describing a collection of entities that have the same attributes: a name and a list of attributes, e.g. EMPLOYEE(Name, Age, Salary). It changes rarely.
    • Entity set: the collection (extension) of all entities of a particular entity type in the database at a particular moment, e.g. {e1=(John Smith,55,80k),e2=(Fred Brown,40,30k),… }\{e_1=(\text{John Smith}, 55, 80\text{k}), e_2=(\text{Fred Brown}, 40, 30\text{k}),\dots\}{e1​=(John Smith,55,80k),e2​=(Fred Brown,40,30k),…}. It changes whenever entities are inserted or deleted.
    • Entity: one member of an entity set, with its own attribute values.

    The entity type is the template, the entity set is the current population of the template, and an entity is one member of that population. (The same name, e.g. EMPLOYEE, is used for both the type and the set.)

    3.5Attribute vs. value setE&N Ex. 3.5 · p. 96

    Explain the difference between an attribute and a value set.

    Solution · written for this guide

    An attribute is a named property of an entity type: formally a function A:E→P(V)A:E\rightarrow P(V)A:E→P(V) that maps each entity eee to a set of values A(e)A(e)A(e) (one value if single-valued, a set if multivalued, the empty set for NULL). A value set (domain) VVV is the set of allowed values for that attribute, e.g. integers 16–70, strings of up to 15 letters.

    The value set says which values are possible; the attribute says what the value means and which entity has which value. Different attributes may share the same value set but differ in meaning: Salary and Bonus can both draw from positive decimals; Age of EMPLOYEE and Age of DEPENDENT both from integers. For a composite attribute the value set is a Cartesian product of the components’ value sets.

    3.6Relationship type, set, instanceE&N Ex. 3.6 · p. 96

    What is a relationship type? Explain the differences among a relationship instance, a relationship type, and a relationship set.

    Solution · written for this guide
    • Relationship type RRR among entity types E1,…,EnE_1,\dots,E_nE1​,…,En​: the schema-level definition of a set of associations among entities of those types, with a name, participating types (and roles), structural constraints and possibly attributes. E.g. WORKS_FOR between EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT, N:1.
    • Relationship set: the current set of associations of that type, R⊆E1×⋯×EnR\subseteq E_1\times\cdots\times E_nR⊆E1​×⋯×En​ (the extension; changes over time).
    • Relationship instance: one member r=(e1,…,en)r=(e_1,\dots,e_n)r=(e1​,…,en​) of the set, associating one entity from each participating type, e.g. (Smith, Research).

    The parallel with entities: relationship type ↔\leftrightarrow↔ entity type, relationship set ↔\leftrightarrow↔ entity set, relationship instance ↔\leftrightarrow↔ entity. Because it is a set, the same combination (e1,…,en)(e_1,\dots,e_n)(e1​,…,en​) cannot appear twice.

    3.7Participation rolesE&N Ex. 3.7 · p. 96

    What is a participation role? When is it necessary to use role names in the description of relationship types?

    Solution · written for this guide

    A role is the function an entity of a participating type plays in each instance of the relationship; the role name names it. In WORKS_FOR, EMPLOYEE plays the role employee (worker) and DEPARTMENT plays department (employer).

    Role names are not needed when all participating entity types are distinct: the entity type name can serve as the role name. They are necessary when the same entity type participates more than once, i.e. in a recursive relationship, to say which participation means what: in SUPERVISION(EMPLOYEE, EMPLOYEE), the instance (e1,e2)(e_1,e_2)(e1​,e2​) is meaningless unless we know that e1e_1e1​ plays supervisor and e2e_2e2​ plays supervisee. They are also useful (not mandatory) when two different relationships link the same two entity types (EMPLOYEE manager of DEPARTMENT vs. EMPLOYEE worker in DEPARTMENT).

    3.8Two notations for structural constraintsE&N Ex. 3.8 · p. 96

    Describe the two alternatives for specifying structural constraints on relationship types. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Alternative 1: cardinality ratio + participation

    Cardinality ratio (1:1, 1:N, M:N) on each edge gives the maximum number of instances an entity can be in (1 or many); participation (total = double line, partial = single line) gives the minimum (at least one, or zero).

    Alternative 2: (min, max) on each participation

    A pair (min⁡,max⁡)(\min,\max)(min,max) written next to entity type EEE, 0≤min⁡≤max⁡0\le\min\le\max0≤min≤max, max⁡≥1\max\ge1max≥1: each entity of EEE is in at least min and at most max instances of RRR. min =0=0=0 is partial, min ≥1\ge1≥1 is total.

    Ratio + participation(min, max)
    Advantagescompact; standard Chen notation; ratio tells you how to map (FK on the N side, separate relation for M:N)more precise: any bounds (“4 to N employees”, “2 to 4 courses”); one uniform notation for both constraints; applies uniformly to n-ary relationships
    Disadvantagesonly distinguishes 0 vs. ≥1\ge1≥1 and 1 vs. many; cannot say “at most 3”; ratio on n-ary relationships is hard to readeasy to misread: written next to the entity it constrains, i.e. on the opposite side from the ratio’s “1”; for n>2n>2n>2 it does not identify the key of the relationship; less widely used by tools

    Example: WORKS_FOR as EMPLOYEE N===1 DEPARTMENT (both total) is, in (min,max), EMPLOYEE (1,1)—(4,N) DEPARTMENT; the “at least 4 employees” cannot be expressed in the first notation.

    3.9Migrating relationship attributesE&N Ex. 3.9 · p. 96

    Under what conditions can an attribute of a binary relationship type be migrated to become an attribute of one of the participating entity types?

    Solution · written for this guide

    An attribute can migrate to entity type EEE only if each entity of EEE participates in at most one relationship instance (max =1=1=1 on EEE’s side), because then the attribute value is determined by the EEE entity alone.

    • 1:1: to either side. Start_date of MANAGES →\rightarrow→ DEPARTMENT (Mgr_start_date) or EMPLOYEE.
    • 1:N: only to the N-side entity type. Start_date of WORKS_FOR (EMPLOYEE N : 1 DEPARTMENT) →\rightarrow→ EMPLOYEE, since each employee works for one department; not to DEPARTMENT, which has many employees with different start dates.
    • M:N: never. Hours of WORKS_ON depends on the (employee, project) combination.

    Even when allowed, it is the designer’s choice; if the receiving side has partial participation the migrated attribute will be NULL for non-participating entities.

    3.10Relationships as attributesE&N Ex. 3.10 · p. 96

    When we think of relationships as attributes, what are the value sets of these attributes? What class of data models is based on this concept?

    Solution · written for this guide

    A binary relationship RRR between E1E_1E1​ and E2E_2E2​ can be seen as an attribute of E1E_1E1​ whose values refer to entities of E2E_2E2​ (and/or the inverse attribute on E2E_2E2​).

    • If each E1E_1E1​ entity is related to at most one E2E_2E2​ entity, the attribute is single-valued and its value set is the entity set E2E_2E2​ itself. EMPLOYEE.Department has value set = the DEPARTMENT entity set.
    • If it can be related to many, the attribute is multivalued and its value set is the power set of the entity set, P(E2)P(E_2)P(E2​): DEPARTMENT.Employees takes as value a subset of the EMPLOYEE entity set.

    If both directions are represented, the two attributes must be inverses of each other. The class of models built on this view is the functional data models (relationships as functions / reference attributes); object (ODMG) data models use the same idea with inverse reference attributes.

    3.11Recursive relationshipsE&N Ex. 3.11 · p. 96

    What is meant by a recursive relationship type? Give some examples of recursive relationship types.

    Solution · written for this guide

    A recursive (self-referencing) relationship type is one in which the same entity type participates more than once, in different roles; role names are then mandatory. Examples:

    RelationshipEntity typeRolesRatio
    SUPERVISIONEMPLOYEEsupervisor, supervisee1:N
    MENTORSRESEARCHERmentor, mentee1:N
    PREREQUISITECOURSEcourse, prerequisiteM:N
    MARRIED_TOPERSONhusband, wife (spouse)1:1
    COMPONENT_OFPARTassembly, component (bill of materials)M:N
    REFERRED_BYCUSTOMERreferrer, referee1:N
    3.12Weak entitiesE&N Ex. 3.12 · p. 96

    When is the concept of a weak entity used in data modeling? Define the terms owner entity type, weak entity type, identifying relationship type, and partial key.

    Solution · written for this guide

    When used: when some entities have no key of their own: they can be identified only in combination with another entity they depend on, and they cannot exist without it (existence dependency). Typical: dependents of an employee, sections/installments/rooms numbered 1, 2, 3 within something, seasons of a TV show.

    • Weak entity type: an entity type with no key attribute; identified by its owner plus its partial key. Double rectangle; total participation in its identifying relationship. DEPENDENT.
    • Owner (identifying) entity type: the entity type whose entities identify the weak entities. EMPLOYEE.
    • Identifying relationship type: the relationship relating the weak entity type to its owner (double diamond). It is 1:N (or 1:1) from owner to weak, with the weak side total, i.e. (1,1). DEPENDENTS_OF.
    • Partial key (discriminator): the attribute(s) of the weak entity that uniquely identify weak entities related to the same owner entity (dashed underline). Dependent Name, assuming no two dependents of one employee share a name. Full identifier: (Essn, Name).

    Not every existence-dependent entity is weak: DRIVER_LICENSE depends on PERSON but has its own key.

    3.13Identifying relationship of degree >2>2>2?E&N Ex. 3.13 · p. 96

    Can an identifying relationship of a weak entity type be of a degree greater than two? Give examples to illustrate your answer.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Yes. A weak entity type may have several owner entity types, and then its identifying relationship has degree >2>2>2: the weak entity is identified by the combination of all its owners plus its partial key. Example (Fig. 3.19): a candidate can have several interviews with the same company (different departments or dates). INTERVIEW is weak, its owners are CANDIDATE and COMPANY via the ternary identifying relationship CCI, and its partial key is Dept_date(Department, Date). An interview is identified by (candidate Name, company Cname, Department, Date). A job offer RESULTS_IN from one interview.

    Further examples: SUPPLY represented as a weak entity with three owners SUPPLIER, PART, PROJECT (Fig. 3.17(c), there via three binary identifying relationships and no partial key); the experiment RUN of the theory section, owned by RESEARCHER, ALGORITHM and DATASET with partial key Run_timestamp.

    3.16SECTION uniqueness constraints (UNIVERSITY, Fig. 3.20)E&N Ex. 3.16 · p. 96

    Which combinations of attributes have to be unique for each individual SECTION entity in the UNIVERSITY database shown in Figure 3.20 to enforce each of the following miniworld constraints:

    1. During a particular semester and year, only one section can use a particular classroom at a particular DaysTime value.
    2. During a particular semester and year, an instructor can teach only one section at a particular DaysTime value.
    3. During a particular semester and year, the section numbers for sections offered for the same course must all be different.

    Can you think of any other similar constraints?

    Figure 3.20 (relevant part): SECTION(SecId, SecNo, Sem, Year, DaysTime, CRoom(Bldg, RoomNo)); COURSE(CCode, CoName, Credits, Level, CDesc) SECS SECTION with COURSE (0,N), SECTION (1,1); INSTRUCTOR(Id, …) TEACHES SECTION with INSTRUCTOR (0,N), SECTION (1,1); STUDENT TAKES SECTION with STUDENT (0,N), SECTION (5,N), attribute Grade.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The instructor and the course of a section are not attributes of SECTION in Fig. 3.20 but come from the relationships TEACHES and SECS. Since SECTION has (1,1) in both, each section has exactly one instructor and one course, so they behave like single-valued attributes of SECTION (after mapping they become FKs Instructor_id and CCode in SECTION). Why: an ER key cannot include a relationship, so (b) and (c) are enforced on the mapped SECTION relation (or as a constraint note on the diagram).
    2. DaysTime values are standard, non-overlapping slots. Why: a uniqueness constraint only prevents equal values; overlapping slots (“MWF 9–9:50” vs. “MW 9–10:15”) would need a separate check.
    ConstraintMust be uniqueSource of attributes
    (a) one section per room per slot{\{{Sem, Year, CRoom(Bldg, RoomNo), DaysTime}\}}all attributes of SECTION
    (b) one section per instructor per slot{\{{Sem, Year, DaysTime, Instructor Id}\}}Id via TEACHES
    (c) distinct section numbers per course{\{{Sem, Year, SecNo, CCode}\}}CCode via SECS

    Each of these is a (candidate) key of SECTION in addition to the surrogate SecId (cf. Exercise 3.26).

    Other similar constraints

    • A student cannot take two sections at the same DaysTime in the same Sem/Year: {\{{Student Sid, Sem, Year, DaysTime}\}} unique among TAKES instances (with the section’s Sem/Year/DaysTime).
    • A student cannot enrol in two sections of the same course in one semester: {\{{Sid, CCode, Sem, Year}\}} unique.
    • (Not a uniqueness constraint, but similar in spirit) enrolment of a section must not exceed the room capacity; an instructor teaches at most kkk sections per semester.
    3.17A nested (complex) attribute for previous educationE&N Ex. 3.17 · p. 97

    Composite and multivalued attributes can be nested to any number of levels. Suppose we want to design an attribute for a STUDENT entity type to keep track of previous college education. Such an attribute will have one entry for each college previously attended, and each such entry will be composed of college name, start and end dates, degree entries (degrees awarded at that college, if any), and transcript entries (courses completed at that college, if any). Each degree entry contains the degree name and the month and year the degree was awarded, and each transcript entry contains a course name, semester, year, and grade. Design an attribute to hold this information. Use the conventions in Figure 3.5.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Start and end dates are single dates per college entry; “if any” means the Degree and Transcript sets may be empty. Why: the question says so.

    Figure 3.5 convention: ( ) = composite, { } = multivalued

    {Previous_college( College_name, Start_date, End_date,
                   {Degree( Degree_name, Month, Year )},
                   {Transcript( Course_name, Semester, Year, Grade )} )}

    Previous_college is multivalued (one entry per college) and composite; inside each entry, Degree and Transcript are again multivalued composite attributes.

    The same attribute drawn in ER notation

    Answer

    {Previous_college(College_name, Start_date, End_date, {Degree(Degree_name, Month, Year)}, {Transcript(Course_name, Semester, Year, Grade)})}: a multivalued composite attribute containing two multivalued composite components.

    3.22Sports league: teams, players, gamesE&N Ex. 3.22 · p. 98★ Must-do

    A database is being constructed to keep track of the teams and games of a sports league. A team has a number of players, not all of whom participate in each game. It is desired to keep track of the players participating in each game for each team, the positions they played in that game, and the result of the game. Design an ER schema diagram for this application, stating any assumptions you make. Choose your favorite sport (e.g., soccer, baseball, football).

    Solution · written for this guide

    Sport chosen: football (soccer), one league season.

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Each team has a unique Team_name; each player a unique Player_id; each game a unique Game_no. Why: names of players repeat, so a surrogate id is safer; games are numbered by the league.
    2. A player belongs to exactly one team during the season (no transfers), and a team registers at least 11 players. Why: then “for which team a player played in a game” is determined by PLAYS_FOR and need not be stored again. (If transfers are allowed, make PLAYED_IN a ternary PLAYER–GAME–TEAM relationship.)
    3. Every game is between exactly two different teams, one home and one away, modelled as two relationships so each game has (1,1) in each. Why: a single M:N TEAM–GAME relationship could not say “exactly two” or which side is home. (“Home team ≠\neq= away team” cannot be drawn in ER; it is stated as a constraint.)
    4. The result is stored as the score (composite: Home_goals, Away_goals); Result (home win/draw/away win) is derived from it.
    5. A player may play several positions in one game (e.g. moved from midfield to defence), so Positions is a multivalued attribute of the relationship PLAYED_IN; it cannot migrate to PLAYER or GAME because PLAYED_IN is M:N.
    6. Each game has between 22 (two starting elevens) and 32 (each side may add up to 5 substitutes) participating players. Why: gives exact (min,max); use (22,N) if substitution rules are unknown.

    Justification of each (min,max)

    • HOME / AWAY: TEAM (0,N): a team plays many home (away) games, possibly none yet early in the season; GAME (1,1): every game has exactly one home and exactly one away team.
    • PLAYS_FOR: TEAM (11,N): at least a starting eleven registered; PLAYER (1,1): one team per player (A2). Shirt_no is a relationship attribute (it could migrate to PLAYER, the 1-side being TEAM).
    • PLAYED_IN: PLAYER (0,N): a squad player may never get on the pitch, or play many games; GAME (22,32) (A6). Positions (multivalued), Minutes and Goals depend on the (player, game) pair, so they stay on the M:N relationship.

    “For each team” is answered by PLAYED_IN joined with PLAYS_FOR (A2); the result by GAME.Score/Result.

    What a marker checks on an ER design question (IA2/GA2 rubrics)

    Every strong entity has an underlined key; (min,max) is a pair on every relationship end and is read as “this entity takes part in min..max instances”; no min >>> max; relationship attributes on M:N relationships are not pushed into an entity; at least one multivalued or composite attribute shown with the right symbol; derived attributes dashed; every non-obvious choice (two teams per game, transfers, positions per game) written as an assumption with a reason. Typical deductions: modelling “position” as a single attribute of PLAYER (it is per game); a single M:N TEAM–GAME relationship without saying how “exactly two teams” is enforced; (min,max) for GAME written on the TEAM side.

    3.26Composite keys of SECTIONE&N Ex. 3.26 · p. 101

    Consider an entity type SECTION in a UNIVERSITY database, which describes the section offerings of courses. The attributes of SECTION are Section_number, Semester, Year, Course_number, Instructor, Room_no (where section is taught), Building (where section is taught), Weekdays (domain is the possible combinations of weekdays in which a section can be offered {‘MWF’, ‘MW’, ‘TT’, and so on}), and Hours (domain is all possible time periods during which sections are offered {‘9–9:50 a.m.’, ‘10–10:50 a.m.’, …, ‘3:30–4:50 p.m.’, ‘5:30–6:20 p.m.’, and so on}). Assume that Section_number is unique for each course within a particular semester/year combination (that is, if a course is offered multiple times during a particular semester, its section offerings are numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on). There are several composite keys for section, and some attributes are components of more than one key. Identify three composite keys, and show how they can be represented in an ER schema diagram.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. A room hosts at most one section at a given (Weekdays, Hours) in a semester, and an instructor teaches at most one section at a given (Weekdays, Hours) in a semester. Why: physical impossibility; these are the rules of Exercise 3.16(a),(b).
    2. Weekdays/Hours values do not partially overlap (a fixed timetable grid). Why: a key can only forbid equal values.

    The three composite keys

    1. K1. {\{{Course_number, Section_number, Semester, Year}\}}: given in the question (section numbers restart per course per semester). Minimal: drop Course_number and two courses can both have section 1; drop Semester or Year and section 1 repeats every term.
    2. K2. {\{{Building, Room_no, Semester, Year, Weekdays, Hours}\}}: one section per room per time slot (A1). Minimal: without Building, rooms with the same number in different buildings clash; without Hours/Weekdays, a room is used for many sections a day.
    3. K3. {\{{Instructor, Semester, Year, Weekdays, Hours}\}}: one section per instructor per time slot (A1). Minimal for the same reasons.

    Semester and Year occur in all three keys; Weekdays and Hours occur in K2 and K3.

    ER representation

    Each key is shown as a composite attribute with its name underlined, whose components are the key’s simple attributes. Because components are shared, the same simple attribute oval is attached to several composite key attributes:

    (Line colours only separate the three keys for reading.) Strictly, standard ER notation attaches each component to one composite attribute, so the shared components would have to be repeated under each key, which duplicates Semester and Year. A cleaner practical design (the one used in Fig. 3.20) is to add a surrogate key Sec_id and record K1–K3 as additional uniqueness constraints (UNIQUE in SQL after mapping). Instructor and Course_number are references to INSTRUCTOR and COURSE; when they are modelled as relationships (TEACHES, SECS), K1 and K3 are no longer expressible as ER keys and become constraints (Exercise 3.16).

    Answer

    K1 = {\{{Course_number, Section_number, Semester, Year}\}}, K2 = {\{{Building, Room_no, Semester, Year, Weekdays, Hours}\}}, K3 = {\{{Instructor, Semester, Year, Weekdays, Hours}\}}; each drawn as an underlined composite attribute of SECTION whose components are the key attributes (shared components attached to several keys).

    9  Chapter 4 exercises (EER)

    Textbook exercises

    Notation used in every diagram of this section

    Specialization: superclass  —  circle with d (disjoint) or o (overlapping); a double line from the superclass to the circle means total, a single line partial. Each subclass line carries the subset mark (∪\cup∪ turned to open towards the superclass). A specialization with one subclass is drawn without a circle. Category (union type): circle with ∪\cup∪; the superclasses join the circle, and the subset-marked line goes from the circle to the category (double = total category). (min,max) is written on the line next to the entity it describes: “this entity takes part in at least min and at most max relationship instances” (the course’s GA2/IA2 convention, and the book’s Section 3.7.4). Double lines mark total participation (min ≥1\ge 1≥1). Key attributes are underlined; partial keys have a dashed underline. The course rubrics speak of a “triangle” joining superclass and subclasses (the drawing tool’s shape); the book’s circle is the same construct. Whatever shape you draw, the d/o letter and the subset marks must be there.

    4.2EER vocabularyE&N Ex. 4.2 · p. 135

    Define the following terms: superclass of a subclass, superclass/subclass relationship, IS-A relationship, specialization, generalization, category, specific (local) attributes, and specific relationships.

    Solution · written for this guide
    TermDefinition (with the example from the figure below)
    Superclass of a subclassThe entity type SSS on which a subclass CCC is defined. Every member of CCC must also be a member of SSS, so C⊆SC \subseteq SC⊆S always holds. EMPLOYEE is the superclass of SECRETARY.
    Superclass/ subclass relationshipThe relationship between a superclass and one of its subclasses (also class/subclass or supertype/subtype relationship). At the instance level it is 1:1: a subclass member and its superclass member are the same real-world entity playing a more specific role. An entity cannot exist only in the subclass. EMPLOYEE/SECRETARY is one such relationship.
    IS-A relationshipAnother name for the superclass/subclass relationship, from the way it is read: “a SECRETARY is an EMPLOYEE”.
    SpecializationThe top-down process of defining a set of subclasses of an entity type, based on some distinguishing characteristic of its entities. Also the resulting set: {SECRETARY, ENGINEER} is a specialization of EMPLOYEE based on job type. Subclasses may get their own attributes and relationships.
    GeneralizationThe reverse, bottom-up process: suppress the differences between several entity types, pick out their common features, and generalize them into one superclass of which the original types are subclasses. CAR and TRUCK (both with Vehicle_id, Price, License_plate_no) are generalized into VEHICLE.
    Category (union type)A subclass of the union of two or more superclasses that may be different entity types. Each member of the category is a member of (at least) one of the superclasses, and it inherits only from the superclass it belongs to (selective inheritance). OWNER ⊆\subseteq⊆ PERSON ∪\cup∪ COMPANY.
    Specific (local) attributesAttributes that belong to a subclass only, and apply only to its members. Typing_speed of SECRETARY, Eng_type of ENGINEER.
    Specific relationshipsRelationship types in which only the members of a subclass take part. MANAGES between MANAGER and PROJECT (an ordinary EMPLOYEE does not manage projects).
    Answer

    Superclass = the set the subclass is a subset of; superclass/subclass (IS-A) relationship = the 1:1 link between an entity’s superclass and subclass roles; specialization = top-down definition of subclasses; generalization = bottom-up merging of entity types into a superclass; category = subclass of a union of different superclasses; specific attributes/relationships = those that apply only to a subclass’s members.

    4.6Constraints on specialization and generalizationE&N Ex. 4.6 · p. 135★ Must-do

    Discuss the two main types of constraints on specializations and generalizations.

    Solution · written for this guide

    1. Disjointness constraint (d or o in the circle).

    • Disjoint (d): an entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. An attribute-defined specialization on a single-valued attribute is automatically disjoint.
    • Overlapping (o): the same entity may be a member of more than one subclass. (The book treats overlap as the default when no disjointness constraint is given.)

    2. Completeness (totalness) constraint (double or single line from superclass to circle).

    • Total: every superclass entity must belong to at least one subclass. Double line.
    • Partial: a superclass entity may belong to no subclass. Single line.

    The two constraints are independent, giving four combinations:

    CombinationMeaning per entityExample (book)
    Disjoint, totalin exactly one subclassEMPLOYEE →\to→ {HOURLY_EMPLOYEE, SALARIED_EMPLOYEE}: every employee is paid one way
    Disjoint, partialin at most one subclassEMPLOYEE →\to→ {SECRETARY, TECHNICIAN, ENGINEER}: other job types exist
    Overlapping, totalin one or more subclassesPART →\to→ {MANUFACTURED_PART, PURCHASED_PART}: some parts are both
    Overlapping, partialin zero or more subclassesPERSON →\to→ {EMPLOYEE, ALUMNUS, STUDENT} (Fig. 4.7)

    Consequences (insertion/deletion rules).

    • Deleting an entity from a superclass deletes it from every subclass it belongs to.
    • Inserting an entity into a superclass inserts it into every predicate-defined (attribute-defined) subclass whose predicate it satisfies.
    • Inserting an entity into the superclass of a total specialization forces it into at least one subclass.

    A superclass obtained by generalization is usually total, because it was formed from the subclasses and holds only their members.

    Answer

    (1) Disjointness: d = an entity is in at most one subclass, o = it may be in several. (2) Completeness: total = every superclass entity is in at least one subclass (double line), partial = it need not be (single line). They are independent, so there are four combinations.

    Watch out

    Mixing the two up: “total” is about whether every superclass entity is in some subclass; “disjoint” is about how many subclasses it can be in. Justify each with a one-line test (“can one employee be both hourly and salaried? No ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ d”); the GA2 rubric checks for it.

    4.7Specialization hierarchy vs latticeE&N Ex. 4.7 · p. 135

    What is the difference between a specialization hierarchy and a specialization lattice?

    Solution · written for this guide
    Specialization hierarchySpecialization lattice
    ConstraintEvery subclass takes part as a subclass in only one class/subclass relationship (one parent).A subclass may be a subclass in more than one class/subclass relationship (several parents).
    ShapeA tree.A lattice (a directed acyclic graph).
    InheritanceSingle inheritance only.Multiple inheritance through the shared subclass; an attribute reached through two paths is inherited only once.
    ExampleFigure 4.1: EMPLOYEE with {SECRETARY, TECHNICIAN, ENGINEER}, {MANAGER}, {HOURLY_, SALARIED_EMPLOYEE}.Figure 4.6: Figure 4.1 plus ENGINEERING_MANAGER, a subclass of ENGINEER, MANAGER and SALARIED_EMPLOYEE.

    In both, a subclass inherits from all its predecessors up to the root. A single shared subclass is enough to turn a hierarchy into a lattice. A shared subclass’s superclasses all share the same root (an engineering manager is one EMPLOYEE); this is what separates it from a category, whose superclasses can be different entity types and whose members are in the union, not the intersection.

    Answer

    In a hierarchy each subclass has exactly one superclass (tree, single inheritance); in a lattice a subclass may have several superclasses (shared subclass, multiple inheritance), e.g. ENGINEERING_MANAGER under ENGINEER, MANAGER and SALARIED_EMPLOYEE.

    4.16Design your own EER schemaE&N Ex. 4.16 · p. 136

    Design an EER schema for a database application that you are interested in. Specify all constraints that should hold on the database. Make sure that the schema has at least five entity types, four relationship types, a weak entity type, a superclass/subclass relationship, a category, and an nnn-ary (n>2n>2n>2) relationship type.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Chosen application: a HOSPITAL. People (doctors and patients) are stored once as PERSON; doctors work in wards; wards contain beds; patients occupy beds; doctors prescribe medicines to patients; patients’ bills are paid by a payer, which may be a person or an insurance company.

    Checklist against the question.

    RequiredWhere it is in the design
    ≥5\ge 5≥5 entity typesPERSON, DOCTOR, PATIENT, WARD, BED, MEDICINE, INSURANCE_COMPANY, PAYER, BILL (9)
    ≥4\ge 4≥4 relationship typesWORKS_IN, HAS_BED, OCCUPIES, PRESCRIBES, FOR, PAYS (6)
    Weak entity typeBED, owner WARD, partial key Bed_no, identifying relationship HAS_BED
    Superclass/subclassPERSON →\to→ {DOCTOR, PATIENT}, overlapping, total
    CategoryPAYER ⊆\subseteq⊆ PERSON ∪\cup∪ INSURANCE_COMPANY (partial)
    nnn-ary, n>2n>2n>2PRESCRIBES (DOCTOR, PATIENT, MEDICINE), ternary, with Rx_date and Dosage

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Every person stored is a doctor or a patient (or both), so PERSON →\to→ {DOCTOR, PATIENT} is total; it is overlapping because a doctor can also be admitted as a patient. Why: the hospital keeps no other people.
    2. A doctor is attached to exactly one ward; a ward may have no doctors yet. Why: ward-based staffing.
    3. Bed numbers restart in each ward (Bed 1 of Ward A, Bed 1 of Ward B), so BED is weak: Ward_no + Bed_no identify it. Why: that is how hospitals label beds.
    4. OCCUPIES records the current admission: a patient occupies at most one bed and a bed holds at most one patient. Why: keeps the example simple; history would need an ADMISSION entity.
    5. A prescription is one doctor prescribing one medicine to one patient on a date, hence ternary; any of the three can appear in many prescriptions or none. Why: the three are needed together to state who prescribed what to whom; three binary relationships would lose that.
    6. Each bill is for exactly one patient and is paid by at most one payer (unpaid bills have none). PAYER is a partial category: only people and companies who have paid a bill become payers. Why: payers are of two different entity types with different keys, which is what a category models.
    7. Age is derived from Dob; Phone is multivalued; Name is composite.

    All constraints that should hold.

    1. C1. Keys: Pid (PERSON, inherited by DOCTOR and PATIENT), Ic_id, Ward_no, Med_code, Bill_no; BED is identified by (Ward_no, Bed_no). Licence_no is also unique among doctors (a secondary key).
    2. C2. Specialization: PERSON →\to→ {DOCTOR, PATIENT} overlapping, total. Category: PAYER ⊆\subseteq⊆ PERSON ∪\cup∪ INSURANCE_COMPANY, partial; a PAYER inherits Pid or Ic_id depending on which superclass it comes from (selective inheritance).
    3. C3. Structural (min,max): as on the diagram, e.g. a DOCTOR works in exactly one WARD (1,1); a BED belongs to exactly one WARD (1,1, identifying); a BILL is for exactly one PATIENT (1,1); each PAYER has paid at least one bill (1,N).
    4. C4. Semantic constraints not shown in the diagram: Dosage >0>0>0; Admit_date ≤\le≤ today; a doctor may not prescribe to himself or herself (the DOCTOR and PATIENT of a PRESCRIBES instance must have different Pid); Bill_date ≥\ge≥ the patient’s Admit_date.
    Answer

    Nine entity types (including weak BED, subclasses DOCTOR/PATIENT and category PAYER), six relationship types including the ternary PRESCRIBES, with every (min,max), key and specialization constraint shown in the diagram, and the remaining semantic constraints listed as C4.

    What the grader checks (IA2 / GA2 EER rubrics)

    Core requirements: (1) a superclass/subclass hierarchy with d or o beside it, every subclass joined to the circle/triangle and not straight to other entities; (2) a weak entity as a double box with a dashed-underlined partial key, joined to its owner by a double diamond, with (1,1) on the weak side and (0,N)/(1,N) on the owner side; (3) a (min,max) pair on every relationship end (“1:N”, “N” or “1” alone is a major mistake); (4) d/o that make sense (test: can one entity be in two subclasses?). Minor and major mistakes are as listed in the IA2/GA2 rubric box at the end of the theory part. For this exercise also check the counts asked for (5 entity types, 4 relationships, a category, an nnn-ary relationship): list them explicitly as above.

    4.17BANK schema with specializationE&N Ex. 4.17 · p. 136★ Must-do

    Consider the BANK ER schema in Figure 3.21 [sic: the BANK schema is Figure 3.22], and suppose that it is necessary to keep track of different types of ACCOUNTS (SAVINGS_ACCTS, CHECKING_ACCTS, …) and LOANS (CAR_LOANS, HOME_LOANS, …). Suppose that it is also desirable to keep track of each ACCOUNT’s TRANSACTIONS (deposits, withdrawals, checks, …) and each LOAN’s PAYMENTS; both of these include the amount, date, and time. Modify the BANK schema, using ER and EER concepts of specialization and generalization. State any assumptions you make about the additional requirements.

    Figure 3.22 (the BANK schema) contains: BANK(Code, Name, Addr)  — 1 BRANCHES N (identifying) —  weak BANK_BRANCH(Branch_no, Addr); BANK_BRANCH 1 ACCTS N ACCOUNT(Acct_no, Balance, Type) with ACCOUNT total; BANK_BRANCH 1 LOANS N LOAN(Loan_no, Amount, Type) with LOAN total; ACCOUNT M A_C N CUSTOMER(Ssn, Name, Phone, Addr) with ACCOUNT total; LOAN M L_C N CUSTOMER with LOAN total.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. The question says “Figure 3.21”, which is the AIRLINE schema; the BANK schema is Figure 3.22 (Exercise 3.23). We modify Figure 3.22. Why: only that figure has ACCOUNT and LOAN.
    2. The existing Type attributes of ACCOUNT and LOAN become the defining attributes of attribute-defined specializations. They are disjoint (Type is single-valued: an account is savings or checking) and partial, because the “…” in the question says other account and loan types exist that we do not model as subclasses.
    3. The question gives no subclass-specific attributes, so we add one per subclass to justify it: Interest_rate (savings), Overdraft_limit (checking), Vehicle_reg_no (car loan), Property_addr (home loan). Why: a subclass with no local attribute or relationship is not needed.
    4. A transaction has no meaning without its account and is numbered within that account, so TRANSACTION is a weak entity owned by ACCOUNT, partial key Trans_no. Likewise PAYMENT is weak, owned by LOAN, partial key Payment_no. Each has Amount, Date, Time.
    5. DEPOSIT, WITHDRAWAL, CHECK are a disjoint, partial specialization of TRANSACTION on Trans_type (one transaction is of one kind; “…” allows others, e.g. transfers). CHECK has the specific attribute Check_no.
    6. Generalization: SAVINGS/CHECKING (and CAR/HOME loans) are what was generalized into the existing ACCOUNT (LOAN) entity, which keeps the common attributes and relationships (A_C, ACCTS). We do not generalize TRANSACTION and PAYMENT into one superclass even though both have Amount, Date, Time, because they are weak entities with different owners (ACCOUNT vs LOAN) and different partial keys; a common superclass would need its own owner. (This is a design choice; a group that does it must state it.)
    7. The ratios and participations of Figure 3.22 are kept and rewritten as (min,max): total = min 1.

    Defining attribute and values are written in italics on the specialization lines (attribute-defined specialization).

    What changed relative to Figure 3.22

    1. ACCOUNT specialized (d, partial, on Type) into SAVINGS_ACCT and CHECKING_ACCT with local attributes.
    2. LOAN specialized (d, partial, on Type) into CAR_LOAN and HOME_LOAN with local attributes.
    3. New weak entity TRANSACTION (owner ACCOUNT, identifying HAS_TRANS, (1,1) on the weak side), itself specialized (d, partial, on Trans_type) into DEPOSIT, WITHDRAWAL, CHECK.
    4. New weak entity PAYMENT (owner LOAN, identifying HAS_PAYMT, (1,1) on the weak side).
    5. All participation/ratio constraints rewritten as (min,max); every subclass inherits Acct_no / Loan_no and the relationships A_C, ACCTS, L_C, LOANS.
    Answer

    Specialize ACCOUNT into {SAVINGS_ACCT, CHECKING_ACCT} and LOAN into {CAR_LOAN, HOME_LOAN} (both disjoint, partial, attribute-defined on Type); add weak entities TRANSACTION (owner ACCOUNT, specialized into DEPOSIT/WITHDRAWAL/CHECK) and PAYMENT (owner LOAN), each with Amount, Date, Time, as in the diagram.

    What the grader checks

    A modification question is graded like a design: the original schema must still be all there (BANK, weak BANK_BRANCH, the four relationships with their constraints), plus the new constructs. Marks are lost for: subclasses with no d/o or no completeness choice; d/o not justified; TRANSACTION/PAYMENT not identified (no key or partial key); a weak entity whose identifying relationship has min 0 on the weak side; missing (min,max). Using Figure 3.21 by mistake is a common slip: say which figure you modified.

    4.18Olympic facilitiesE&N Ex. 4.18 · p. 136

    The following narrative describes a simplified version of the organization of Olympic facilities planned for the summer Olympics. Draw an EER diagram that shows the entity types, attributes, relationships, and specializations for this application. State any assumptions you make.

    The Olympic facilities are divided into sports complexes. Sports complexes are divided into one-sport and multisport types. Multisport complexes have areas of the complex designated for each sport with a location indicator (e.g., center, NE corner, and so on). A complex has a location, chief organizing individual, total occupied area, and so on. Each complex holds a series of events (e.g., the track stadium may hold many different races). For each event there is a planned date, duration, number of participants, number of officials, and so on. A roster of all officials will be maintained together with the list of events each official will be involved in. Different equipment is needed for the events (e.g., goal posts, poles, parallel bars) as well as for maintenance. The two types of facilities (one-sport and multisport) will have different types of information. For each type, the number of facilities needed is kept, together with an approximate budget.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Each COMPLEX has a surrogate key Complex_id; the chief organizer is stored as an attribute (Chief_organizer), not an entity. Why: the narrative gives no details about organizers.
    2. COMPLEX →\to→ {ONE_SPORT, MULTISPORT} is disjoint and total, attribute-defined on Ctype. Why: “complexes are divided into one-sport and multisport types”: every complex is exactly one of them.
    3. A ONE_SPORT complex records its single Sport. A MULTISPORT complex has a multivalued composite attribute Areas{Sport, Loc_indicator}, one value per sport area. Why: areas have no identity or relationships of their own in the narrative.
    4. “For each type, the number of facilities needed and an approximate budget” is information about the type, not about each complex. EER has no class-level attributes, so it is modelled as an entity FACILITY_TYPE (two instances: one-sport, multisport) with Num_needed and Approx_budget, linked to each complex by OF_TYPE. Why: putting these on every complex would repeat the same value many times.
    5. Every event is held in exactly one complex; a complex may hold many events (possibly none yet). Events have a surrogate key Event_id.
    6. No_officials is derived (count of OFFICIATES instances for the event). No_participants is stored (athletes are not modelled). Why: the officials roster is kept anyway.
    7. The roster: every listed official is involved in at least one event (1,N); an event needs at least one official (1,N).
    8. EQUIPMENT is specialized into EVENT_EQUIP and MAINT_EQUIP, overlapping (a ladder can serve an event and maintenance) and total (all equipment is needed for one purpose or the other). Each subclass has its specific relationship: EVENT_EQUIP is USED_IN events (with Quantity), MAINT_EQUIP is NEEDED_FOR the maintenance of complexes.
    Answer

    COMPLEX specialized (d, total, on Ctype) into ONE_SPORT (Sport) and MULTISPORT (multivalued composite Areas); COMPLEX HOLDS EVENT; OFFICIAL OFFICIATES EVENT (M:N roster); EQUIPMENT specialized (o, total) into EVENT_EQUIP (USED_IN EVENT) and MAINT_EQUIP (NEEDED_FOR COMPLEX); per-type count and budget kept in FACILITY_TYPE.

    What the grader checks

    Narrative-to-EER questions are marked on: every noun with data becoming an entity or attribute (complex, event, official, equipment, the two complex types); the specialization drawn with a justified d/o and total/partial; the multisport “areas with location indicator” captured (multivalued composite or a weak entity); the officials roster as an M:N relationship; equipment for events and for maintenance both represented; keys on every strong entity; (min,max) on every relationship end; and a written assumption for each interpretation (for example, how the per-type budget is stored).

    4.19Georgia Tech Library: concepts, constraints and EERE&N Ex. 4.19 · p. 137

    Identify all the important concepts represented in the library database case study described below. In particular, identify the abstractions of classification (entity types and relationship types), aggregation, identification, and specialization/generalization. Specify (min, max) cardinality constraints whenever possible. List details that will affect the eventual design but that have no bearing on the conceptual design. List the semantic constraints separately. Draw an EER diagram of the library database.

    Case Study: The Georgia Tech Library (GTL) has approximately 16,000 members, 100,000 titles, and 250,000 volumes (an average of 2.5 copies per book). About 10% of the volumes are out on loan at any one time. The librarians ensure that the books that members want to borrow are available when the members want to borrow them. Also, the librarians must know how many copies of each book are in the library or out on loan at any given time. A catalog of books is available online that lists books by author, title, and subject area. For each title in the library, a book description is kept in the catalog; the description ranges from one sentence to several pages. The reference librarians want to be able to access this description when members request information about a book. Library staff includes chief librarian, departmental associate librarians, reference librarians, check-out staff, and library assistants.

    Books can be checked out for 21 days. Members are allowed to have only five books out at a time. Members usually return books within three to four weeks. Most members know that they have one week of grace before a notice is sent to them, so they try to return books before the grace period ends. About 5% of the members have to be sent reminders to return books. Most overdue books are returned within a month of the due date. Approximately 5% of the overdue books are either kept or never returned. The most active members of the library are defined as those who borrow books at least ten times during the year. The top 1% of membership does 15% of the borrowing, and the top 10% of the membership does 40% of the borrowing. About 20% of the members are totally inactive in that they are members who never borrow.

    To become a member of the library, applicants fill out a form including their SSN, campus and home mailing addresses, and phone numbers. The librarians issue a numbered, machine-readable card with the member’s photo on it. This card is good for four years. A month before a card expires, a notice is sent to a member for renewal. Professors at the institute are considered automatic members. When a new faculty member joins the institute, his or her information is pulled from the employee records and a library card is mailed to his or her campus address. Professors are allowed to check out books for three-month intervals and have a two-week grace period. Renewal notices to professors are sent to their campus address.
