    The library does not lend some books, such as reference books, rare books, and maps. The librarians must differentiate between books that can be lent and those that cannot be lent. In addition, the librarians have a list of some books they are interested in acquiring but cannot obtain, such as rare or out-of-print books and books that were lost or destroyed but have not been replaced. The librarians must have a system that keeps track of books that cannot be lent as well as books that they are interested in acquiring. Some books may have the same title; therefore, the title cannot be used as a means of identification. Every book is identified by its International Standard Book Number (ISBN), a unique international code assigned to all books. Two books with the same title can have different ISBNs if they are in different languages or have different bindings (hardcover or softcover). Editions of the same book have different ISBNs.

    The proposed database system must be designed to keep track of the members, the books, the catalog, and the borrowing activity.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. BOOK means a title (one ISBN); VOLUME means a physical copy. A copy is numbered within its ISBN, so VOLUME is a weak entity (owner BOOK, partial key Copy_no). Why: “100,000 titles and 250,000 volumes”, and the librarians count copies per book.
    2. The catalog is the set of BOOK entities with their Title, Authors, Subjects and Description; there is one catalog, so it is not a separate entity. Authors and Subjects are multivalued attributes (a book can have several). Why: the narrative stores nothing about authors or subjects themselves.
    3. Borrowing history must be kept (“borrowing activity”, “borrow at least ten times during the year”), and the same member can borrow the same volume twice. A plain M:N MEMBER–VOLUME relationship cannot hold two instances for the same pair, so a loan is an entity LOAN (Loan_no, Date_out, Due_date, Date_returned).
    4. Lendability is a property of the title (reference books, rare books and maps are never lent): BOOK →\to→ {LENDABLE, NON_LENDABLE} is disjoint, partial (a wanted title we do not hold is neither). WANTED_BOOK (titles the library wants to acquire) is a separate single-subclass specialization of BOOK, since a wanted title may or may not be held already (e.g. lost copies not replaced).
    5. MEMBER is identified by Card_no; Ssn is also unique (a second key). PROFESSOR is a subclass of MEMBER (partial: most members are not professors) with its own loan rules. Card_expiry is derived (issue date + 4 years).
    6. STAFF →\to→ {CHIEF_LIBRARIAN, ASSOC_LIBRARIAN, REF_LIBRARIAN, CHECKOUT_STAFF, LIB_ASSISTANT} is disjoint, total, attribute-defined on Position. Each loan is issued by one check-out staff member. Why: these are the five staff roles listed, and each person holds one position.

    1. Classification (entity types and relationship types)

    Entity typeAttributes (key underlined)
    MEMBERCard_no, Ssn, Name, Campus_addr, Home_addr, {Phones}, Photo, Card_issue_date, Card_expiry (derived)
    PROFESSOR (subclass)Emp_id, Dept
    BOOKISBN, Title, Description, Edition, Language, Binding, {Authors}, {Subjects}, Num_copies (derived), Num_on_loan (derived)
    VOLUME (weak)Copy_no
    LENDABLE, NON_LENDABLE, WANTED_BOOKNON_LENDABLE: Reason (reference / rare / map); WANTED_BOOK: Acq_reason (out of print, lost, …)
    LOANLoan_no, Date_out, Due_date (derived), Date_returned
    STAFF (+ 5 subclasses)Staff_id, Sname, Position
    RelationshipParticipants with (min,max)Meaning
    HAS_COPY (identifying)BOOK (0,N), VOLUME (1,1)a title has 0 or more copies (wanted titles have none); each copy is of one title
    BORROWED_BYMEMBER (0,N), LOAN (1,1)20% of members never borrow, so min 0; each loan is by one member
    OF_VOLUMEVOLUME (0,N), LOAN (1,1)a copy may never have been lent; a loan is of one copy
    ISSUED_BYCHECKOUT_STAFF (0,N), LOAN (1,1)each loan is issued by one check-out staff member

    2. Aggregation

    • Attributes aggregated into an entity: MEMBER = (Card_no, Ssn, Name, addresses, phones, photo, card dates); BOOK = (ISBN, Title, Description, …).
    • An entity aggregated from other objects: LOAN aggregates a MEMBER, a VOLUME, a CHECKOUT_STAFF and the dates; it plays the role of a “relationship with history”.
    • The catalog is an aggregation of BOOK descriptions by author, title and subject.

    3. Identification

    • BOOK by ISBN (Title is explicitly not an identifier: same title, different ISBN for other languages, bindings, editions).
    • VOLUME by (ISBN, Copy_no) through HAS_COPY (weak entity).
    • MEMBER by Card_no (also by Ssn); STAFF by Staff_id; LOAN by Loan_no.

    4. Specialization/generalization

    • MEMBER →\to→ PROFESSOR (partial): different loan period (3 months), grace period (2 weeks), notices to campus address.
    • BOOK →\to→ {LENDABLE, NON_LENDABLE} (d, partial); BOOK →\to→ WANTED_BOOK (partial).
    • STAFF →\to→ five roles (d, total, on Position); CHECKOUT_STAFF has the specific relationship ISSUED_BY.
    • A predicate-defined subclass is possible: ACTIVE_MEMBER = members with ≥10\ge 10≥10 loans in the year. It is derivable from LOAN, so it is not stored.

    5. Details that affect the eventual design but not the conceptual design

    • Volumes: 16,000 members, 100,000 titles, 250,000 volumes (2.5 copies per title), 10% of volumes out on loan.
    • Behaviour statistics: return within 3–4 weeks, 5% of members get reminders, most overdue books back within a month, 5% of overdue books never returned, top 1% / 10% of members do 15% / 40% of the borrowing, 20% inactive.
    • Description length (one sentence to several pages): a storage/data type decision.
    • The online catalog listing by author, title and subject: access paths and indexes.
    • Professors’ data is pulled from employee records; the card is mailed; notices are sent: application processing, not schema.

    These affect physical design (file sizes, indexes, expected load), not which entities and relationships exist.

    6. Semantic constraints (not expressible in the EER diagram)

    1. S1. A member may have at most 5 loans with Date_returned = NULL at any time. (Not a max cardinality: BORROWED_BY is (0,N) over the whole history.)
    2. S2. Due_date = Date_out + 21 days for ordinary members and + 3 months for professors.
    3. S3. A notice is sent when today >>> Due_date + grace (1 week; 2 weeks for professors).
    4. S4. Only volumes of LENDABLE books may appear in a LOAN.
    5. S5. A volume can be in at most one open loan at a time.
    6. S6. Card_expiry = Card_issue_date + 4 years; a renewal notice is sent one month before expiry, to the campus address for professors.
    7. S7. Every professor is a member (automatic membership).
    8. S8. Num_on_loan(book) = number of its volumes in open loans; Num_copies −-− Num_on_loan copies are in the library.

    7. EER diagram

    Answer

    Entity types MEMBER (subclass PROFESSOR), BOOK (title; subclasses LENDABLE/NON_LENDABLE and WANTED_BOOK), weak VOLUME, LOAN, STAFF (five role subclasses); relationships HAS_COPY, BORROWED_BY, OF_VOLUME, ISSUED_BY with the (min,max) above; aggregation, identification and specialization as in steps 2–4; physical-design details in step 5 and semantic constraints S1–S8 in step 6.

    Watch out

    Writing “(0,5)” on MEMBER in BORROWED_BY. The limit of five applies to books out at the same time; across the history a member borrows many times. Keep (0,N) and state the five-book rule as a semantic constraint (S1). Likewise, statistics (16,000 members, 10% on loan) are not constraints.

    4.20Art museum EER schemaE&N Ex. 4.20 · p. 138★ Must-do

    Design a database to keep track of information for an art museum. Assume that the following requirements were collected:

    • The museum has a collection of ART_OBJECTS. Each ART_OBJECT has a unique Id_no, an Artist (if known), a Year (when it was created, if known), a Title, and a Description. The art objects are categorized in several ways, as discussed below.
    • ART_OBJECTS are categorized based on their type. There are three main types—PAINTING, SCULPTURE, and STATUE—plus another type called OTHER to accommodate objects that do not fall into one of the three main types.
    • A PAINTING has a Paint_type (oil, watercolor, etc.), material on which it is Drawn_on (paper, canvas, wood, etc.), and Style (modern, abstract, etc.).
    • A SCULPTURE or a statue has a Material from which it was created (wood, stone, etc.), Height, Weight, and Style.
    • An art object in the OTHER category has a Type (print, photo, etc.) and Style.
    • ART_OBJECTs are categorized as either PERMANENT_COLLECTION (objects that are owned by the museum) and BORROWED. Information captured about objects in the PERMANENT_COLLECTION includes Date_acquired, Status (on display, on loan, or stored), and Cost. Information captured about BORROWED objects includes the Collection from which it was borrowed, Date_borrowed, and Date_returned.
    • Information describing the country or culture of Origin (Italian, Egyptian, American, Indian, and so forth) and Epoch (Renaissance, Modern, Ancient, and so forth) is captured for each ART_OBJECT.
    • The museum keeps track of ARTIST information, if known: Name, DateBorn (if known), Date_died (if not living), Country_of_origin, Epoch, Main_style, and Description. The Name is assumed to be unique.
    • Different EXHIBITIONS occur, each having a Name, Start_date, and End_date. EXHIBITIONS are related to all the art objects that were on display during the exhibition.
    • Information is kept on other COLLECTIONS with which the museum interacts; this information includes Name (unique), Type (museum, personal, etc.), Description, Address, Phone, and current Contact_person.

    Draw an EER schema diagram for this application. Discuss any assumptions you make, and then justify your EER design choices.

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Artist is a relationship, not an attribute. ARTIST is its own entity with many attributes, so the “Artist” of an art object becomes the relationship CREATED_BY. Each object has at most one known artist: ART_OBJECT (0,1), because the artist may be unknown. An artist is stored only if at least one of his/her objects is in the database: ARTIST (1,N).
    2. Type specialization: disjoint, total. OTHER exists “to accommodate objects that do not fall into one of the three main types”, so every object is in some subclass (total), and each object is of one type (disjoint).
    3. SCULPTURE and STATUE have the same attributes but are kept as two subclasses because the requirements name them as separate main types. (Merging them, or generalizing them into a 3D_OBJECT superclass, is an acceptable alternative.) Style is generalized up to ART_OBJECT. The requirements list Style for all four subclasses, and the type specialization is total, so every art object has a Style. Why: one attribute instead of four copies; it is inherited back by every subclass. (Keeping Style in each subclass is also correct.)
    4. Ownership specialization: disjoint, total. “Categorized as either PERMANENT_COLLECTION … or BORROWED”: each object is exactly one of the two.
    5. “The Collection from which it was borrowed” becomes the relationship BORROWED_FROM between BORROWED and COLLECTION, since COLLECTION is an entity: BORROWED (1,1), COLLECTION (0,N) (the museum may interact with a collection it has not borrowed from).
    6. EXHIBITION is identified by Name (assumed unique). DISPLAYED_IN is M:N: an exhibition shows at least one object (1,N); an object may never have been exhibited (0,N).
    7. Year, DateBorn, Date_died may be NULL (unknown / still living); Origin and Epoch are simple single-valued attributes of ART_OBJECT.

    Justification of the design choices

    1. Two independent specializations of ART_OBJECT (by type, by ownership): an object is both, e.g. a borrowed painting. Drawing them as two separate circles keeps each d/total constraint independent.
    2. Specific attributes go into the subclasses so that ART_OBJECT does not carry many NULL columns (a statue has no Paint_type).
    3. ARTIST and COLLECTION as entities, not attributes, because each has its own attributes and a key (Name), and one artist/collection relates to many objects; storing them as attributes would repeat the artist’s data in every object.
    4. BORROWED_FROM is a specific relationship of BORROWED: only borrowed objects come from another collection, so the relationship is attached to the subclass, not to ART_OBJECT (where it would be NULL for every permanent object).
    5. DISPLAYED_IN is M:N because one exhibition shows many objects and one object may be shown at many exhibitions over time.
    Answer

    ART_OBJECT with two disjoint, total specializations: {PAINTING, SCULPTURE, STATUE, OTHER} and {PERMANENT_COLLECTION, BORROWED}; ARTIST via CREATED_BY (object (0,1), artist (1,N)); EXHIBITION via M:N DISPLAYED_IN; COLLECTION via BORROWED_FROM attached to the BORROWED subclass.

    What the grader checks

    This was set in past papers. Marks go to: both specializations with the correct and justified d/o and total/partial (“either … or” ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ d; OTHER exists ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ total); local attributes on the right subclasses; Artist and Collection turned into entities with relationships (keeping “Artist” as a plain attribute of ART_OBJECT loses marks, since ARTIST has its own data); the borrowed-from relationship attached to BORROWED, not ART_OBJECT; keys underlined (Id_no, artist Name, collection Name, exhibition Name); (min,max) on every relationship end; written assumptions and a short justification of each design choice, as the question asks.

    10  Exam cheat sheet

    Entities, attributes, keys

    • Attribute kinds: simple vs composite (hierarchy of components); single- vs multivalued (a set, double oval); stored vs derived (Age from Birth_date, dashed oval); complex = nested ( ) composite and { } multivalued.
    • NULL: not applicable (Apt_no of a house) or unknown. Type vs set: type = schema (intension); set = entities present now (extension).
    • Key attribute: distinct for every entity at every time (property of the type, not today’s data); underlined; may be composite (must be minimal); several keys allowed. No key ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ weak entity.
    • Superkey / candidate / primary: superkey = no two entities agree on it (all attributes always one); candidate = minimal superkey; primary = the chosen candidate (not NULL), others alternate. Primary ⊆\subseteq⊆ candidate ⊆\subseteq⊆ super.
    • Superkey count (nnn attributes; superkey iff it contains some key): one key of size kkk: 2n−k2^{n-k}2n−k.  Several keys: inclusion–exclusion ∑2n−∣Ki∣−∑2n−∣Ki∪Kj∣+⋯\sum 2^{n-|K_i|}-\sum 2^{n-|K_i\cup K_j|}+\cdots∑2n−∣Ki​∣−∑2n−∣Ki​∪Kj​∣+⋯.  mmm single-attribute keys: 2n−2n−m2^n-2^{n-m}2n−2n−m (all non-empty subsets minus those with no key attribute).
    • Checks: STUDENT(SID+4) =24=16=2^4=16=24=16; CAR, two single keys, n=6n=6n=6: 63−15=4863-15=4863−15=48; keys {A,B},{B,C} in n=5n=5n=5: 8+8−4=128+8-4=128+8−4=12. Show formula and arithmetic (bare number: 1/3 marks).
    • Value set: allowed values; attribute = function A:E→P(V)A:E\to P(V)A:E→P(V) (NULL = ∅\emptyset∅).

    Relationship types and constraints

    • Degree = number of participating entity types. Role names are required when a type participates twice (recursive: SUPERVISION supervisor/supervisee).
    • Cardinality ratio: max participations: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. The 1 sits on the edge of the entity that appears once (DEPARTMENT 1 — N EMPLOYEE).
    • Participation: total (every entity takes part, double line, min ≥1\ge1≥1) or partial (single line, min 0).
    • (min,max): beside entity EEE = each EEE is in at least min, at most max instances. It goes on EEE’s own edge, so the max “1” appears on the opposite side from the ratio’s 1.
    Ratio (E1E_1E1​:E2E_2E2​)beside E1E_1E1​beside E2E_2E2​
    1:1(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)
    1:N (E2E_2E2​ has ≤\le≤1 E1E_1E1​)(⋅,N)(\cdot,\mathrm{N})(⋅,N)(⋅,1)(\cdot,1)(⋅,1)
    M:N(⋅,N)(\cdot,\mathrm{N})(⋅,N)(⋅,N)(\cdot,\mathrm{N})(⋅,N)
    partial / total(0,⋅)(0,\cdot)(0,⋅)(1,⋅)(1,\cdot)(1,⋅) or more
    • Example: EMPLOYEE N—1 DEPARTMENT ≡\equiv≡ EMPLOYEE (1,1)—(4,N) DEPARTMENT. Ratio gives the mapping and only 0/1/many; (min,max) is precise but gives no key for n>2n>2n>2.
    • Relationship attribute migration: 1:1 to either side; 1:N only to the N side; M:N never (Hours depends on the (employee, project) pair).

    Weak entity types

    • Definition: no key of its own; identified by owner’s key + partial key (discriminator, dashed underline) via an identifying relationship (double diamond); weak entity = double box.
    • Constraints: weak side total, (1,1); owner-to-weak is 1:N or 1:1; owner side (0,N) or (1,N). Full id: (owner key, partial key), e.g. (Ssn, Dependent Name).
    • Total ⇏\not\Rightarrow⇒ weak: DRIVER_LICENSE depends on PERSON but has its own key, so strong.
    • Variants: owner itself weak; several owners (INTERVIEW). Prefer weak entity over a multivalued composite attribute if it has its own relationships or many attributes.

    ER notation (Chen, Fig. 3.14)

    • Also: composite = oval with child ovals; roles = lowercase edge labels; names ENTITY (singular), RELATIONSHIP (verb), Attribute. No FK attributes in ER (a reference is a relationship). UML multiplicity sits at the opposite end from ER (min,max).

    Ternary vs binary

    • Not equivalent: three binaries CAN_SUPPLY, USES, SUPPLIES lose the ternary fact “sss supplies ppp to jjj”. Keep the ternary plus any binary with independent meaning; binaries replace it only under extra constraints (CAN_TEACH 1:1).
    • Alternatives: weak entity with three identifying relationships (no partial key), or strong entity with surrogate key. Repeated triples (“log every run”): weak entity RUN + partial key Run_timestamp.
    • Ratio on nnn-ary: a 1 on EiE_iEi​ = for fixed other participants, at most one EiE_iEi​; 1-edges drop out of the relationship’s key. All M/N: key is all three.
    • (min,max) on nnn-ary counts triples: TEACHES on PROF, COURSE, STUDENT: 1–2 profs and 1–100 students per course, prof 0–3 courses, student 0–6: COURSE (1,200)(1,200)(1,200), PROF (0,300)(0,300)(0,300), STUDENT (0,12)(0,12)(0,12) (co-teaching assumed). PROF (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) is the classic error.

    EER: subclasses, specialization, constraints

    • Subclass: S⊆CS\subseteq CS⊆C always (IS-A), inherits everything; create one only for local attributes or local relationships. Specialization top-down, generalization bottom-up (usually total).
    • Membership: predicate-defined (condition on the line), attribute-defined (all subclasses on one defining attribute; disjoint if single-valued), user-defined.
    • Disjointness (d/o in the circle): d = at most one subclass; o = may be in several. Test: “can one entity be in two subclasses?”
    • Completeness (superclass–circle line): total = every entity in some subclass (double line); partial = may be in none (single). Independent of d/o: 4 combinations.
    • Hierarchy vs lattice: hierarchy = one superclass per subclass (tree); lattice = some subclass has several (shared subclass, multiple inheritance).

    Shared subclass vs category

    Shared subclassCategory (union)
    Membersin all superclasses (∩\cap∩)in one of them (∪\cup∪)
    Inheritsall superclasses’ attributesonly its own superclass’s (selective)
    Superscommon root, same keydifferent types, different keys
    Drawnsubset lines to each superclassone circle with U
    ExampleENGINEERING_ MANAGEROWNER = PERSON ∪\cup∪ BANK ∪\cup∪ COMPANY
    • Category: total (double line circle–category) = whole union. Generalize instead when the classes share a key; category when keys differ.

    Traps that cost marks

    • (min,max) on the wrong side, or a bare “1:N”, “N”, “1” where a pair is required: major (grade C).
    • Strong entity with no key, weak entity with no partial key, min >>> max: major.
    • Weak entity with min 0 on its weak side or no identifying relationship: major. Single box / single diamond / solid-underlined partial key: minor.
    • d where one entity is in two subclasses (or o where impossible); subclass joined to anything but its circle/superclass; dangling relationship line: major.
    • Minor (3 ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ B): no multivalued/composite attribute; derived not dashed; no assumptions.
    • Total vs disjoint mixed up: total = whether every entity is in a subclass; d = how many.
    • Ternary max counting courses, not triples; “5 books at a time” as max: keep (0,N), state a semantic constraint.
    • M:N attribute pushed into an entity (position per game on PLAYER); ARTIST kept as an attribute.
    • Modification: the original schema must still all be there.

    Exam moves (how the rubric reads a design)

    • 1. Assumptions first: A1, A2, …, each with a one-line why (min values, d/o, total/partial, repeated triples). A defended choice is not penalised.
    • 2. Diagram: key underlined on every strong entity; weak entity double box + double diamond + dashed partial key; at least one composite and one multivalued attribute; derived dashed.
    • 3. Constraints: one convention throughout; a (min,max) pair on every relationship end, read “this entity takes part in min..max instances”; weak side (1,1).
    • 4. EER: d/o and total/partial on every specialization, each with its one-line test (“either … or” ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ d; OTHER subclass ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ total); local attributes and relationships on the subclass.
    • 5. Close: one bullet justifying each (min,max); list any counts asked for; a short “semantic constraints” list for what the diagram cannot show.
